prize_parts.citation: for the theoretical prediction and experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall effect and topological insulators

statement.case_for: Topological insulators are the case on the table where a simple, universal organising idea (a Z2 invariant of time-reversal-symmetric band structures, with protected edge channels) was stated cleanly by theory, confirmed quantitatively by experiment, and then understood and generalised. Kane and Mele supplied the decisive 2005 theory; Molenkamp's group observed the quantised edge conductance in HgTe quantum wells in 2007, a measurement that could have failed and did not. Fifteen years of independent confirmation in two and three dimensions, across many materials and now photonic, acoustic and cold-atom platforms, mean the interpretation is stable. Of the shortlisted fields it is the one in which the mechanism is both identified and well understood, which is the criterion I weigh most. It also draws the broadest support in the room (four top-three rankings, six of eight members ranking it), and six members including me independently proposed the same three names.
statement.case_against: The 2016 prize for topological phase transitions and phases of matter already honoured the conceptual foundation, so the committee must be able to state what is distinct here, namely the time-reversal-invariant Z2 class and its realisation in real materials rather than the integer quantum Hall lineage. Attribution is also genuinely awkward: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe route that Molenkamp's group tested, and Hasan's work on three-dimensional topological insulators is decisive but falls outside a three-name cap that already contains Kane, Mele and Molenkamp. Any triple will be read as a judgement against living claimants.

responses.point: Ranks B034 (magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene) first as a quantitatively predicted new quantum state in a material, tested by experiment, and notes that many groups now reproduce the correlated phases.
responses.response: I agree that Bistritzer-MacDonald is the cleanest prediction on the list, and I ranked it second. But reproducibility of the phenomena is not the same as understanding them: the origin of the superconductivity and the nature of the correlated states are still debated, and sample dependence is real. My own test of whether a breakthrough is understood favours topological insulators, where the mechanism has been settled for over a decade. I would hold B034 back a few years, not reject it, and I keep it as my first alternative.

responses.point: Places circuit QED (B013) first as a mature, widely reproduced platform that is the natural follow-on to the 2025 prize, and ranks the topological insulator case third as mature and arguably overdue.
responses.response: We agree on maturity for B016. On B013 I would qualify the argument: the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is exactly why I hesitate, since two circuit-based awards in two years would need a sharply distinct citation, and the three-name credit omits Girvin and Devoret who are part of the story. Circuit QED is an enabling architecture whose scientific message (strong coupling on a chip) is less of a new organising principle than the Z2 classification. I would be glad to hear whether you think the distinctness argument survives.

responses.point: Puts optical lattice clocks (B059) first as precision atomic physics with a clear idea, good agreement between theory and experiment and a pending redefinition of the second, and ranks topological insulators last of her eight because of the 2016 prize.
responses.response: I take the clocks case seriously: it is clean, two names are essentially uncontested, and it has the strongest support in the room, so I cannot dismiss it. It is outside my own field, so I defer on the metrology. My reservation is the overlap with the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-clock prizes, which makes the incremental conceptual step smaller than it looks. On your 2016 objection to B016, I disagree with the weight: the 2016 citation was about topological phase transitions and the integer quantum Hall lineage, while the time-reversal-invariant class and its experimental realisation in HgTe and Bi-based materials is a separate chain from prediction to observation. Is a stricter overlap test being applied to B016 than to B059?

responses.point: Proposes Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan for B016, arguing that Hasan's first experimental three-dimensional topological insulator work is as decisive as any other contribution, with Mele left out.
responses.response: This is the sharpest attribution disagreement on B016. Mele is a co-author of the Kane-Mele Z2 paper, and leaving out one of two authors of the founding theoretical proposal is hard to defend in the way the 2024 and earlier citations treat joint theory. Hasan's three-dimensional ARPES discovery is real and important, but it is an extension of an idea already realised in two dimensions by Molenkamp's group; I prefer to keep the citation on the prediction and first observation. I would accept that the three-name cap forces an unsatisfactory choice, and the committee should record that Hasan, Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are strong claimants.

responses.point: Ranks optical lattice clocks first and cites independent confirmation and surpassing of the original performance in many laboratories, and ranks squeezed light (B058) fourth while noting its impact is partly an enabling technology for a field already prized in 2017.
responses.response: Your independent-confirmation point for the clocks is right, and it is the same property I credit to topological insulators. Where I would push back is only on how much the possible redefinition of the second adds as scientific weight: it is a metrological milestone rather than a new mechanism. I share your hesitation about squeezed light as an enabling technology, but I would apply the same bar consistently across the shortlist.

uncertainties: Whether the committee views the 2016 topological-phases prize as already covering the Z2 topological insulator, or sees it as a distinct achievement.
How to treat Hasan and the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang HgTe proposal under the three-person cap.

Whether the Kardar-Parisi-Zhang case (B049), which I ranked first and which only I supported in the opening, can be fairly credited without Parisi's contribution or without including exact-solution work by Johansson, Prahofer, Spohn and others.
How much weight maturity of understanding of the superconducting state in twisted bilayer graphene should carry against its rapid influence on the field.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent with the shortlisted candidates from my profile; none of my frequent co-authors is a credited name. Goran Johansson and Eva Olsson are in the Gothenburg physics environment (Chalmers) but I have no specific collaboration with them or with any candidate that would require recusal.
